script.title: How Meesho Makes ₹4,132 Cr Charging 0% Commission

segments.text: How does a company make billions by charging zero percent commission?
While Amazon takes up to twenty-five percent from sellers, Meesho did the exact opposite. They told Indian small businesses to sell for free.
Yet, Meesho just pulled in ₹4,132 crore in revenue for a single quarter. At the same time, they slashed their quarterly loss by 68% down to ₹132 crore.
How do you build a multi-thousand crore paisa engine when your core product costs sellers nothing? Today, we decode Meesho's hidden money machine.
If sellers pay zero commission, where is Meesho actually getting thousands of crores?
The answer starts with advertising. Imagine you sell cheap kurtis in Jaipur alongside ten thousand other sellers.
How do buyers find your shop first? You pay Meesho for ad placement on their search page.
Meesho flipped the model completely. Instead of forcing a sales tax on every product, they turned selling into a competitive bidding game.
Sellers willingly give money for visibility because without ads, their products stay invisible. That advertising engine generates massive high-margin revenue.
The second stream is logistics, powered by their logistics platform called Valmo. Every time a package moves from Surat to Patna, Meesho earns a slice of shipping.
They do not own thousands of trucks themselves. They aggregate local courier partners through clever jugaad and technology.
By charging small logistics margins across millions of daily orders, those tiny drops turn into a massive ocean of cash.
Amazon spent billions targeting metro buyers, but Meesho quietly captured real Bharat.
In big cities, people buy branded smartphones and fancy sneakers online. But in Tier 2 and Tier 3 India, people want unbranded everyday fashion.
The average order value on Meesho is often less than the cost of a couple of auto rides. We are talking about two hundred to three hundred rupees.
At that price point, traditional delivery costs would destroy any business model. A normal courier charge could cost as much as the item itself.
So Meesho engineered a low-cost delivery network specifically built for lower price items. They bundled orders and worked with regional partners who operate on razor-thin margins.

This sharp focus on Bharat helped their order volumes explode, driving quarterly revenue up 34% year on year.
Slashing quarterly losses by 68% sounds amazing, but can Meesho actually become profitable?
For years, Indian startups burned millions on customer acquisition discounts. You gives free cashbacks, customers buy once, and then they leave.
Meesho managed to break that habit by relying on organic word-of-mouth spread across WhatsApp groups and social resellers.
By reducing marketing burn and growing ad revenue, their net loss shrank down to just ₹132 crore.
However, competition is not sitting quiet. Quick commerce apps and rival marketplaces are expanding fast into smaller towns.
As an educational takeaway for young investors, watching a company transition from cash-burn to positive cash flow is the ultimate lesson in unit economics.
Keep in mind this analysis is for educational purposes only and is not financial advice. The big lesson here is simple: zero price to sellers does not mean zero profit for the platform.
